extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students of algebraic geometry (reading Vakil's Math 216 / The Rising Sea)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, equivalent characterizations, and local-check criteria for common scheme-theoretic properties (Proj construction, quasicompactness, reducedness, integrality, normality, factoriality, etc.), presented as exercises and explanatory remarks for students learning to check/build these properties. Emphasis on affine-local (localization/gluing) techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevant ideal / V(I) = ∅ equivalences (Proj)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded ring S• and homogeneous ideal I, the following are equivalent: (a) V(I) = ∅ in Proj S•; (b) the distinguished opens D(fi) (for a set of homogeneous generators fi of I) cover Proj S•; (c) √I ⊃ S+ (i.e., the radical of I contains the irrelevant ideal S+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates calling S+ the “irrelevant” ideal: any ideal whose radical contains S+ is geometrically irrelevant. Use this to detect when a homogeneous ideal cuts out nothing in Proj. (See Exercise 4.5.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: I(Z) is homogeneous and V(I(Z)) = Z (Proj)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a subset Z ⊂ Proj S•, the ideal I(Z) (functions vanishing on Z) is homogeneous and satisfies V(I(Z)) = Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show I(Z) is a homogeneous ideal of S• and check that taking V(–) and I(–) interact as expected on Proj, analogous to the affine case. Use the graded/homogeneous structure in the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski topology restriction to Spec((S•)f)0
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion Spec((S•)f)0 → Proj S• (for homogeneous f) identifies the Zariski topology on the former with the subspace topology induced from Proj S•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to justify gluing: on each distinguished open D(f) in Proj, we want the structure sheaf to be that of Spec((S•)f)0. (See Exercise 4.5.J.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sheaf on Proj by gluing Spec((S•)f)0
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the structure sheaf on Proj S• by giving, for each homogeneous f, the sheaf on D(f) identified with O_{Spec((S•)f)0} and then glue these sheaves using the standard gluing lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: identify pairwise isomorphisms between Spec((S•)fg)0 and distinguished opens of Spec((S•)f)0, check compatibility on triple overlaps, and reinterpret sheaf in terms of compatible stalks. (Exercises 4.5.K–4.5.M, 2.7.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of overlaps: Spec((S•)fg)0 ≅ distinguished open in Spec((S•)f)0
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous f,g, there is an isomorphism Spec((S•)fg)0 ≅ the distinguished open subset D(g^{deg f}/f^{deg g}) of Spec((S•)f)0, and similarly swapping f and g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identifications provide the pairwise gluings needed to assemble the structure sheaf of Proj. Verify compatibility of these identifications on triple overlaps before gluing. (Exercise 4.5.K.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective space definition P^n_A = Proj A[x0,...,xn]
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective n-space over a ring A is defined as P^n_A := Proj A[x0, ..., xn]; the projective coordinates x0,...,xn are part of the definition and the D(xi) cover Proj A[x0,...,xn].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check this agrees with earlier coordinate-based constructions of projective space; the definition avoids messy patch choices. (Definition 4.5.8 and Exercise 4.5.N/O.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing scheme V(f) in Proj when S• generated in degree 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If S• is generated in degree 1 and f ∈ S+ is homogeneous, one can define a closed subscheme V(f) inside Proj S• (though f is not in general a global function on Proj; it should be viewed as a section of a line bundle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret f as a section of an appropriate line bundle and define V(f); extend to V(I) for any homogeneous ideal I. (Exercise 4.5.P and later references to sections of line bundles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective and quasiprojective scheme definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective A-scheme is (isomorphic to) Proj S• for some finitely generated graded ring S• over A. A quasiprojective A-scheme is a quasicompact open subscheme of a projective A-scheme. The base ring A is often omitted when clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: in the Noetherian case quasicompactness requirement is redundant. Many typical geometric examples are projective or quasiprojective over a field. (Definition 4.5.9 and remarks.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompactness equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is quasicompact iff it can be written as a finite union of affine open subschemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to check quasicompactness in practice; e.g., P^n_A is quasicompact because it is covered by finitely many affines D(xi). (Exercise 5.1.D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasicompact schemes have closed points
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a quasicompact scheme, then every point has a closed point in its closure; every nonempty quasicompact scheme has at least one closed point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often used to reduce checking an open-local property to checking it at closed points: if a property P of points is open, to show all points have P it suffices to check closed points for quasicompact schemes. (Important Exercise 5.1.E.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasiseparatedness definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space (or scheme) is quasiseparated if the intersection of any two quasicompact open sets is quasicompact. For schemes: equivalently, intersections of affine opens are finite unions of affines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasiseparatedness is a mild finiteness condition useful in many theorems. Most schemes encountered in practice are quasiseparated (affine, locally Noetherian, separated are all quasiseparated). (Section 5.1.1 and Exercise 5.1.F.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine schemes are quasiseparated
rubrics_metrics.description: Any affine scheme Spec A is quasiseparated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by showing intersections of affine opens in an affine scheme can be covered by finitely many distinguished opens. (Exercise 5.1.G.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective A-schemes are quasicompact and quasiseparated
rubrics_metrics.description: All projective A-schemes are quasicompact and quasiseparated (the graded ring in the definition is finitely generated giving a finite affine cover).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when applying theorems that assume these hypotheses. (Exercise 5.1.I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducedness definition for rings and schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotents. A scheme X is reduced if OX(U) is reduced for every open U ⊂ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent to checking no stalk has nonzero nilpotents; if X is reduced then equal sections that agree on points are equal. (Definition 5.2.1 and Exercise 5.2.A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducedness is stalk-local
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme is reduced iff all its stalks have no nonzero nilpotents (i.e., reducedness can be checked on stalks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets you check reducedness on affine opens or closed points in quasicompact situations. (Exercise 5.2.A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: For quasicompact schemes, reducedness can be checked at closed points
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is quasicompact, it suffices to check reducedness at closed points: any nonreduced point has a nonreduced closed point in its closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume reducedness is an open condition in general; use Exercise 5.1.E to reduce to closed points. (Exercise 5.2.D and Remark 5.2.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reducedness need not be an open condition
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist schemes whose reduced locus is not Zariski-open (construct pathological examples with infinitely many nilpotent supports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware: in locally Noetherian schemes the reduced locus is open, but in general it need not be. (Remark 5.2.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrality definition and criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is integral if it is nonempty and for every nonempty open U, OX(U) is an integral domain. Equivalently, X is irreducible and reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral schemes have a generic point η; the stalk at η is the function field K(X). For integral X, restriction maps to any nonempty open are inclusions into K(X). (Definition 5.2.4 and Exercise 5.2.F–I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Function field and injectivity of restriction maps (integral schemes)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is integral with generic point η and Spec A is a nonempty affine open, OX,η identifies with K(A) (fraction field), and for any nonempty open U the map OX(U) → OX,η = K(A) is an inclusion; hence restriction maps among nonempty opens are inclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes gluing sections on integral schemes easy: sections are equal iff they are the same element of K(X). (Exercises 5.2.H–I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrality almost stalk-local (Noetherian case)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Noetherian (or locally Noetherian) settings integrality can be characterized by local stalk conditions plus connectedness: X is integral iff X is nonempty, connected, and all stalks OX,p are integral domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to check integrality by local data in good (Noetherian) situations. (Exercise 5.3.C.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine Communication Lemma (afﬁne-local property test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A property P of affine opens is affine-local if (i) whenever Spec A has P then all distinguished opens Spec Af have P (stability under localization), and (ii) if (f1,...,fn)=A and each Spec Afi has P then Spec A has P (gluing from distinguished opens). If a scheme has a cover by affine opens with P then every affine open subset has P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central tool to decide whether a scheme property can be checked on an affine cover. Use it to reduce scheme-level checks to affine algebra. (Affine Communication Lemma 5.3.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking reducedness/Noetherian/finite-generation afﬁne-locally (Proposition 5.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Reducedness: A reduced implies Af reduced; if each Af_i reduced then A reduced. (b) Noetherian: same pattern for Noetherian property. (c) Finite generation over a base B: preserved under localization and can be checked on a cover by distinguished opens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete instances of affine-local properties; use the lemma to deduce scheme-level statements from affine checks. (Proposition 5.3.3.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally Noetherian / Noetherian scheme definitions and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is locally Noetherian if it can be covered by affine opens Spec A with A Noetherian. If in addition X is quasicompact (finite such cover) then X is Noetherian. Consequences: underlying topological space Noetherian, all open subsets quasicompact, and several finiteness results follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language is used throughout; many theorems assume locally Noetherian or Noetherian hypotheses to use finiteness. (Definition 5.3.4 and remarks.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian schemes have finitely many irreducible/connected components
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian scheme has a finite number of irreducible components; it also has finitely many connected components, each a finite union of irreducible components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful structural fact for arguments that use irreducible decomposition in the Noetherian case. (Exercise 5.3.B.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: A-schemes, locally of finite type, finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-scheme is a scheme where all structure sheaf rings are A-algebras and restriction maps are A-algebra maps. X is locally of finite type over A if it has an affine cover by finitely generated A-algebras; of finite type if quasicompact in addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This organizes schemes relative to a base ring; being (locally) finite type over a ring implies locally Noetherian when the base is Noetherian. (Section 5.3.6.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety definitions (affine/projective/quasiprojective k-varieties)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affine k-variety is an affine scheme that is reduced and of finite type over k. A (quasi)projective k-variety is a reduced (quasi)projective k-scheme of finite type. Note literature variations: sometimes irreducible is also required or k assumed algebraically closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions connect schemes to classical algebraic geometry. Check radicalness of defining ideals when characterizing affine varieties. (Exercise 5.3.D and surrounding remarks.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Normality definition and basics
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is normal if all its stalks OX,p are integrally closed domains (i.e., integral and integrally closed in their fraction fields). Normality implies reducedness but need not imply integrality globally (disjoint unions can be normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use localization properties: integral closure is preserved by localization, so to check normality it often suffices to check appropriate local rings (closed points in quasicompact situations). (Section 5.4.1 and Exercise 5.4.A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral closure preserved under localization
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an integrally closed domain and S is a multiplicative subset not containing 0, then S^{-1}A is integrally closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows checking integrally-closed (normal) property at local rings and reduces global normality checks to local ones. (Exercise 5.4.A.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian normal scheme structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian scheme is normal iff it is a finite disjoint union of integral Noetherian normal schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a structural characterization helpful when working under Noetherian hypotheses; normality may be checked on components. (Exercise 5.4.B.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Check integral closure at primes/maximals (Proposition 5.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integral domain A, A is integrally closed iff Ap is integrally closed for all prime ideals p, and equivalently iff Am is integrally closed for all maximal ideals m ⊂ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus it suffices to check integral closure at localizations at primes or even maximal ideals. Proof uses the ideal of denominators construction. (Proposition 5.4.2.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Factoriality (locally factorial) definition and remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A scheme X is factorial if all of its stalks are unique factorization domains (often called locally factorial). If A is a UFD then Spec A is factorial; the converse need not hold (there exist factorial schemes with no affine cover by UFDs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factoriality implies normality. The locus of factorial points can be open in certain contexts (e.g., varieties over an algebraically closed field). Check by finding appropriate affine covers when possible, but be aware covers by UFDs need not exist. (Definition 5.4.4, Exercises 5.4.E and 5.4.5.)
